Spent the morning on something I think is bigger than a side demo, and it touches all our layers — so bringing it here first before anything goes public.

I ran a full agent-service consultation end to end, live on-chain: a consumer consults a forensic agent, gets a verifiable report, and pays for it — every leg independently checkable, and nothing in the running stack was modified.

- the report came from a real ERC-8004 agent (NFT-bound identity)
- it's bound to the query in a WYRIWE commitment (recompute-verifiable): 0x8c798f43…
- payment settled on Sepolia with that commitment in the calldata: 0x925ea5e7e4716601796a3f78133b1b6e69d860fb531aca18b4f5456bafaef7e3 — so the payment is provably tied to that exact report, not just "a payment"

The point: this composes all of our work in one transaction — 8004 identity, 8281/8299 input provenance, 8274 verify, 8263 anchor, ReceiptOS eligibility, 8275 settlement, the task layer as the spine. It's the end-to-end story we've each been building a piece of, and I don't think anyone's shown it composing live yet.

So rather than ship it as a dinamic.eth thing, I think it's worth far more as a shared reference flow — a composition note, same format as the 8004 + 8263 + OCP one. It also answers the two open questions on the 28785 thread directly: Ankita's "what's the unit of accountability across multi-agent workflows" and KBryan's "common execution envelope."

And don't take my word for any of it — the agents I set up for you are live on dinamic.eth and the tooling is UI-configurable, so do your own research. Configure your agent's tools in the UI and run it, or hit its MCP endpoint directly to consult the forensic agent the way I did — agent-to-agent calls go through the MCP endpoint with the A2A headers, and the gateway already does the trust + signature checks. @Damon you've also got a ccip-router node, so you can point an agent at that too. Honestly the best way to judge whether this composes is to run your own agent through it.

Drafted the note — it credits every layer, and each of you owns the step that's yours; I'll hold the integration. Want to formalize this together? If we're aligned I'll circulate it for edits before it goes anywhere public.

an idea that crystallised working the ERC-1833 thread — I think we’ve been building one thing from several angles, and it’s worth naming.

The pattern: verifiable economics for specialized MCP agents. A specialized agent (forensic, recovery, consultation, trading) acts on a user’s behalf through MCP tools. For that to be safe AND paid, four properties have to hold, each recomputable from public data:

identity — who the agent is, bound to which account → ERC-8004 (+ source-token binding)
bounded authority — how much it may consume, metered before it acts, per scope → ERC-1833 (blockbird’s cursor/envelope)
witnessed action — each action a recomputable signed proof → WYRIWE (8299) + 8274
owner-bound, settle-once settlement — value only to the owner’s address, gated on the witness, replay-nullified → the recovery escrow / ConsultEscrow / 8275 settlement axis
The realization: the recovery escrow Fede and I shipped is a sharp instance of (3)+(4) for a single action. ERC-1833 is (2) — the same gate generalized to bounded authority across many actions/accounts. And a live specialized agent (e.g. the forensic agent on dinamic.eth, MCP-driven) needs all four at once. So it’s not four projects — it’s one stack, most of which we already have, with 1833 filling the bounds layer we didn’t need for one action but do for a real agent.

1 — capabilityRoot provenance: yes, 8004 identity + the accepted 8001 mandate. capabilityRoot[agent] = the agent’s commitment to the per-scope sub-budget tree derived from the mandate it accepted, so the cursor never invents authority — only spends down what 8001 granted. 2 — leaf encoding: keccak(scopeId, subCap, agentId) is the right v1, but “max 1/counterparty” needs a counterparty dimension. I’d make the leaf a typed envelope — { scopeId, subCap, asset, agentId, dims? } — so a richer profile adds counterparty / time-window / asset caps without changing the gate. Keep the simple leaf as the baseline, same way blockbird kept the flat budget profile.

3 — nullifier sharing: this is the one I’d flag a footgun on. A draw-once and a settle-once are different invariants. In our recovery escrow they looked like one event because there’s one action = one settlement — but a real multi-action agent draws authority N times under a mandate and may settle separately (per-action, or once at the end). If the cursor and the escrow share a single registry keyed on receiptId, the first leg to run nullifies it and the second reverts. So I’d not collapse them to one key. Either (a) one registry, namespaced — keccak(receiptId,"draw") vs keccak(receiptId,"settle") — or (b) separate registries with an explicit link. “one draw == one settlement” only holds in the single-action case; the metering layer is exactly where it stops holding.

4 — base commitment (@DamonZwicker’s layer): the witness’s “recomputable” claim bottoms out at OCP (8281) — receiptId/receiptProof are recomputable because the verdict commits via observation → digest → on-chain commitment → verify-inclusion. The stack proves a verdict is faithful: committed before the outcome, recomputable from public data, no trusted party. What it cannot prove is that the observation scope was complete. ### Step 4 - Verify (ERC-8274, anchored via ERC-8263): conformance criteria

The verify step establishes that a named validator examined the step's input and issued a verdict
that was committed before the outcome the verdict is graded against. Verification establishes
AUTHENTICITY, never SOUNDNESS: a conformant verify answers "is this authentically the named
validator's verdict over exactly this input", and MUST NOT be read as "the action is sound".

A verify step is conformant if and only if all of the following hold, each checkable from public
data with no trust in the validator or any intermediary:

1. Binding. The verdict's prove MUST bind its three facts (the input judged, the verdict issued,
   and the action gated) so that none can be substituted after the fact. Concretely, the verdict
   commits to the inputHash it judged, and binds to the gated step through the DAG predecessor
   linkage (a gating step's outputHash becomes the gated step's inputHash, and the gated step's
   stepHash commits to prevStepHashes). A verdict carrying a different inputHash than the step it
   gates is non-conformant.

2. Pre-commitment (the committed_at gate). The verdict's committed_at MUST be provably prior to the
   outcome it is graded against, anchored to a system the validator does not control (an on-chain
   anchor or equivalent). Ordering enforced only by the handler at execution time is NOT sufficient
   on its own when the graded outcome is external to the workflow (a settlement, a P&L, a reveal).

3. Type discriminator. The reference point for condition 2 is set by judgment_type:
   - outcome_verifiable (Type A): committed_at MUST precede the realized outcome's settlement.
   - consensus_weighted (Type B): committed_at MUST precede the reveal.

4. Gating, not observation. A non-approving verdict for a gating step MUST halt progression: the
   handler MUST reject any subsequent step that lists the gating step in its predecessors. A verify
   step whose verdict is advisory only, and does not gate, is post-hoc attestation, not pre-action
   verification.

5. Recomputable, not issuer-asserted. Every property above MUST be recomputable by any party from
   public data and the validator's published key: recompute the proof's id, check the signature
   against that key, and check the anchored committed_at against the outcome. The step MUST NOT rely
   on a trusted issuer asserting its own eligibility, correctness, or timing.

Granularity is an implementation choice. Two implementations MAY draw step boundaries differently;
as long as each step's prove satisfies conditions 1 through 5, the audit guarantee is identical. The
guarantee lives in the binding, not the slicing. (This is the conformance form of the answer to
Ankita's unit-of-accountability question.)

@GobRoss @babyblueviper1 I’m thinking about our previously discussed code audit requirements. Is it viable to adopt agent-based auditing? We could form a wager agreement, requiring the auditing agent to stake bond collateral to assume liability. I’d love to hear your thoughts on this idea.

Short answer: viable and worth doing — but bonded auditing only holds up if the bond rides on top of recomputability, not in place of it. Otherwise a stake is just an attestation in disguise ("trust my verdict, I put money behind it"), which is the same trusted-party shape we argued against on the witness side: you end up trusting the richest staker, and a well-capitalized bad actor self-insures.

The version that works is three layers, with the bond only ever carrying the residual:

1. Recomputable proof for everything mechanizable — re-execution, signature vs a published key, commit-before-outcome. The bond is never at risk for anything a third party can just re-check, so it is not insuring re-checkable facts.

2. The bond covers the irreducible judgment — "is this code actually secure / this audit actually thorough" — the part that is not mechanically recomputable. That is also exactly who should be on the hook: whoever is liable for being wrong.

3. The slash condition itself has to be recomputable, and this is the clean part: the bond slashes when someone nominates a provable missed vuln — an omission. That is Damon scope-contestation axis as-is: faithfulness != completeness, an honest miss settles clean unless someone can nominate it. So bonded auditing is not a new primitive, it is witness (8299/8274) + settle-once escrow (8275) + scope-contestation, composed.

Two things worth naming up front: a bond makes an audit accountable, not correct (liability != correctness — it aligns incentives and gives recourse, it does not produce truth), and the bond has to scale with value-at-risk or auditors rationally eat the slash on rare misses.

Jimmy — sharpest question anyone's put to it, and it lands exactly on the seam the registry stops at by design.
You're right that F★ is always relative to a classification function w, and w is a choice someone makes. So a bare nomination — "X wasn't in the declared scope" — is w-independent and not falsifiable on its own. It's a permanent dispute record by design: the registry is non-adjudicating precisely because it can't know F★ without w, and w isn't its to fix.
The falsifiable upgrade is the path you named, and it has a precise shape. A nomination of X becomes falsifiable as material (X ∈ F★ under w) when you can exhibit a witness pair (a, b) where w(a) ≠ w(b), a and b agree on every declared coordinate (indistinguishable in the committed scope), and they differ on X. That pair is cryptographic proof the declared scope can't separate a case w must separate, and that X is what closes the gap — the on-chain instance of observational sufficiency failing.
And your condition is the necessary one: the witness pair only carries weight if w is publicly recomputable, because the verifier has to check w(a) ≠ w(b) itself. If w is private, w(a) ≠ w(b) is an assertion and you're back to a bare dispute. Two layers:

Layer 1 (this registry): was X observed? — w-independent, always falsifiable, what's built.
Layer 2 (witness-pair contestation over public w): did X matter? — w-relative, falsifiable only if w is publicly computable.

The honest part, and why it can't collapse into one layer: w itself is contestable. A different w gives a different F★. Making w public doesn't end the regress — it relocates it. Materiality becomes falsifiable relative to a named, public w, and disagreement about which w is correct becomes its own higher-order contestation. That's the most you get without a trusted party, and it's the right amount: the chain certifies "X separates a witness pair under this w," never "this w is the correct w."
So yes — Layer 2 is real, it's the next primitive, and publicly-computable w is its precondition. Want to spec it as the companion axis?

@JimmyShi22 — Layer 2 classifier reads clean. Giving w its own stateless IScopeClassifier instead of overloading IAgentVerifier is the right call: w-recompute over a witness pair and agent-output verification are different relations, and keeping params as the object of consensus — one deployed classifier, N markets, params *is* w — is the factoring that makes it reusable without a contract per market. The two reference classifiers (continuous/mad+median, categorical/majority) cover the space well.

Four notes on the classifier itself — all impl-level, none structural:

1. Continuous precision / double-rounding. Median of an even-count set lands on a half-ULP — (34.9 + 35.0)/2 = 34.95 at precision 0.1. If the aggregate is held at the committed precision before the final quantize, you round twice and can cross the threshold on the rounding alone. Worth stating in w's definition that internal aggregation scale must exceed precision, with exactly one quantize at the comparison.

2. Continuous gas. median and MAD both need sorting; on-chain that's O(n log n), and for large minSamples it's a real gas/griefing surface. Either cap sample count in params validation or document the bound. Categorical is fine — counting is linear.

3. Pin the classifier, not just params. "params is the object of consensus" is right, but params alone doesn't pin w — the classifier *address* has to be committed too, or w can be reshaped by swapping the contract after the outcome is observable, which defeats the pre-commit MUST. The commitment should be (scopeRoot, classifier, paramsHash), not (scopeRoot, paramsHash). Tiago's Layer2PreCheck already binds the address in the Market struct — worth lifting into the spec text so it's normative rather than impl-only.

4. Classifier-internal reverts. The require()s inside classify (minSamples, filtered > 0) revert opaquely; custom errors let an off-chain re-deriver tell which precondition tripped. Minor.

@babyblueviper1 — right seam, and worth going one level finer, because the membership check is necessary but won't fully close it.

Your completeness check (every a.sourceId ∈ scopeRoot, |a| = N) closes the *coordinate* half — a is over the declared id-set, nothing smuggled in. But it leaves the *value* half open: scopeRoot's leaves are id-only (leaf = keccak(0x00‖c)) and it's committed at market creation, before the readings exist — so it can't pin a's values even in principle. A contester who satisfies completeness can still choose adversarial values on the declared coords and manufacture separation. (Concretely: an a with all N declared sources present but votes set to a boundary split passes membership and still flips under one added X.)

So two halves:
- coordinate-completeness (your check, against scopeRoot) — necessary;
- value-fidelity (a reproduces the committed readings) — needs a *resolution-time* commitment, since scopeRoot structurally can't carry it.

That's the fork in the normative text: membership alone gets "X is material to some coordinate-complete a" (a robustness claim); adding the value commitment gets "X was material to *the* resolution" (what the prose reads like). If it's the latter, contest() wants both guards — completeness against scopeRoot, plus a's values checked against a resolution commitment — both require()-style, both before classify, neither touching params.
